title: Trees: structure, answers, and work
description: Build and trace subtree answers, mirror a hierarchy at every level, search for the first matching path, count traversal work, then produce a shipment report.

learned: State what a completed recursive call returns for its own subtree.
Tell structure from labels: a leaf is a node with no children.
Build a new tree from child results without changing the original.
Stop a search at the first match, and count the work a traversal really does.
recap.invariant: Each completed call returns a correct answer for exactly its own subtree.
recap.complexity: Whole-tree aggregation: Θ(n) time and O(h) recursive stack space with constant-time selectors and bounded-size arithmetic; drawing is excluded.
recap.common_mistake: Deciding the base case from a label (such as label == 1 or a falsy label) instead of from an empty child sequence.
in_real_programs: Python ast.iter_child_nodes exposes immediate child nodes for syntax-tree traversal.

retrieval.question: Module 4: what does using selectors protect?
retrieval.answer: Clients depend on the interface instead of the concrete representation.

exercises.title: Build: how deep does it go?
exercises.prompt_md:
Implement `height(t)`: the number of nodes on the longest path from this node down to a leaf. A single node has height 1 whatever its label; the hierarchy in the demo has height 3. Use the selectors `label`, `branches` and `is_leaf`, never the dictionary keys.

The function also receives `path` and `whole` so that it can draw. When you descend into child number `i`, pass `path + (i,)` and the same `whole`. Call `show(whole, path, result)` exactly once per call, after that call knows its answer. Each frame then shows one completed subtree and its height. Before you press Run, decide which node completes first and which completes last.

checklist.step: Return the height on varied shapes and labels
Record each completed subtree with its true height

tests.name: structural_height
tests.code:
show = lambda *args: None
assert height(tree(0)) == 1, "A single node has height 1, even when its label is 0."
assert height(tree(1, [tree(0)])) == 2, "A node with one child has height 2, whatever the labels are."
assert height(tree(5, [tree(5), tree(5), tree(5), tree(5)])) == 2, "Four children side by side add width, not height."
assert height(tree(1, [tree(2), tree(3, [tree(4, [tree(5)])])])) == 4, "The longest path may run through a later child: take the largest child answer, not the first."

import random
rng = random.Random(611)
def make(depth):
    return tree(rng.randrange(-4, 5), [make(depth - 1) for _ in range(rng.randrange(4))] if depth else [])

def oracle(t):
    best, pending = 0, [(t, 1)]
    while pending:
        node, depth = pending.pop()
        best = max(best, depth)
        pending.extend((c, depth + 1) for c in node["children"])
    return best
for _ in range(40):
    t = make(rng.randrange(5))
    got = height(t)
    assert got == oracle(t), f"Expected height {oracle(t)} for a random hierarchy, got {got}: combine the child answers with max, then count this node."

tests.name: completion_frames
tests.code:
from scimigo import _frame_count, _frame
before = _frame_count()
assert height(sample) == 3, "The demo hierarchy has height 3: root, child 1, and one of its children."
expected = [((0,), 1), ((1, 0), 1), ((1, 1), 1), ((1,), 2), ((2,), 1), ((), 3)]
recorded = _frame_count() - before
assert recorded == len(expected), f"Record one completion frame per node: 6 nodes, {recorded} frames."
for offset, (path, value) in enumerate(expected):
    objects = _frame(before + offset)
    figures = [o for o in objects if o['kind'] == 'figure']
    assert figures and figures[0]['type'] == 'tree', "Draw the hierarchy in each completion frame (call show)."
    node = sample
    for i in path: node = branches(node)[i]
    name = 'root' if not path else '.'.join(map(str, path))
    assert figures[0]['params']['highlights'] == {name + ':' + str(label(node)): 'current'}, f"Frame {offset + 1} should highlight {name}: children complete before their parent, left to right."
    assert any(o['kind'] == 'text' and o['value'] == 'Completed ' + name + ': ' + str(value) for o in objects), f"Frame {offset + 1} should show height {value} for the subtree at {name}."

hints: Decide what one completed call promises: the height of exactly its own subtree.
Look at a leaf first. It has no children, so what must it return, and does its label matter?
An internal node is one node taller than its tallest child. Ask every child, keep the largest answer, then count the node itself.

exercises.title: Trace: when answers become available
exercises.prompt_md:
`totals(t)` returns the sum of every label in the hierarchy, internal labels included. Answer the two predictions first, on paper, from the demo hierarchy drawn by the starter: root 4 with children 7, 0 and -3, where the child labelled 0 has two children labelled 9.

Then implement `totals`. Pass `path + (i,)` and `whole` when you descend, and call `show(whole, path, result)` once per call, after that call's sum is known. The frames show completion, not entry into a call. Step through them and compare the order with your prediction.

questions.prompt: What does the call on the root return?

choices.why: This adds only the root and its three children: 4 + 7 + 0 - 3. The two 9s are deeper.
This adds only the leaves: 7 + 9 + 9 - 3. Internal labels count too.
All six labels: 4 + 7 + 0 + 9 + 9 - 3.

questions.prompt: Which node completes immediately before the root?

choices.why: It is the first to complete; two more subtrees follow it.
The root waits for all three children, and the last child finishes last.
It completes after its own two children, but child 2 is still to come.

checklist.step: Match every completion frame to its subtree sum
Handle deeper hierarchies and a single node

tests.name: trace_answers
tests.code:
from scimigo import _frame_count, _frame
before = _frame_count()
got = totals(sample)
assert got == 26, f"The six labels 4, 7, 0, 9, 9 and -3 sum to 26; totals returned {got}."
expected = [((0,), 7), ((1, 0), 9), ((1, 1), 9), ((1,), 18), ((2,), -3), ((), 26)]
recorded = _frame_count() - before
assert recorded == len(expected), f"Record one completion frame per node: 6 nodes, {recorded} frames."
for offset, (path, value) in enumerate(expected):
    objects = _frame(before + offset)
    figures = [o for o in objects if o['kind'] == 'figure']
    assert figures and figures[0]['type'] == 'tree', "Draw the hierarchy in each completion frame (call show)."
    node = sample
    for i in path: node = branches(node)[i]
    name = 'root' if not path else '.'.join(map(str, path))
    assert figures[0]['params']['highlights'] == {name + ':' + str(label(node)): 'current'}, f"Frame {offset + 1} should highlight {name}: a node completes only after all of its children."
    assert any(o['kind'] == 'text' and o['value'] == 'Completed ' + name + ': ' + str(value) for o in objects), f"Frame {offset + 1} should show the subtree sum {value} at {name}."

tests.name: other_totals
tests.code:
show = lambda *args: None
assert totals(tree(3, [tree(4, [tree(-10)])])) == -3, "Include descendants at every depth: 3 + 4 - 10 = -3."
assert totals(tree(0)) == 0, "Zero is a valid label; a single node sums to its own label."

import random
rng = random.Random(622)
def make(depth):
    return tree(rng.randrange(-4, 5), [make(depth - 1) for _ in range(rng.randrange(4))] if depth else [])

def oracle(t):
    total, pending = 0, [t]
    while pending:
        node = pending.pop()
        total += node["value"]
        pending.extend(node["children"])
    return total
for _ in range(30):
    t = make(4)
    got = totals(t)
    assert got == oracle(t), f"Expected label sum {oracle(t)} on a random hierarchy, got {got}."

hints: A completed call's answer covers its whole subtree, so a parent cannot finish before its children.
List the nodes in the order their calls return, not the order they start. Which call returns last?
Start from the node's own label, add the answer of each child in order, and only then record the frame.

exercises.title: Implement: mirror every level
exercises.prompt_md:
Implement `deep_reverse(t)`. It returns a **new** hierarchy with the same labels in which the children of every node appear in the opposite order: at the root, and inside every child, all the way down. The input must be left exactly as it was, and the result must not share any node with it.

The demo draws the original and then whatever your function returns. In the original, node names such as `1.0:9` read position, then label. In a correct mirror the root's children read -3, 0, 7 from the left, and the two grandchildren read 2, 9. Reversing only the root's children leaves them as 9, 2.

checklist.step: Reverse the children at every level
Return fresh nodes and leave the input unchanged

tests.name: mirrored_everywhere
fresh_structure
tests.code:
show_tree = lambda *args: None
import copy

import random
rng = random.Random(634)
def make(depth):
    return tree(rng.randrange(-4, 5), [make(depth - 1) for _ in range(rng.randrange(4))] if depth else [])

def nodes(t):
    found, pending = [], [t]
    while pending:
        node = pending.pop()
        found.append(node)
        pending.extend(node["children"])
    return found
for _ in range(20):
    t = make(4)
    original = copy.deepcopy(t)
    result = deep_reverse(t)
    assert t == original, "Leave the input unchanged: build new nodes instead of reversing its child lists in place."
    old = {id(n) for n in nodes(t)} | {id(n["children"]) for n in nodes(t)}
    assert all(id(n) not in old and id(n["children"]) not in old for n in nodes(result)), "The result must not share nodes or child lists with the input."
    assert deep_reverse(result) == original, "Mirroring twice must give back the original shape and labels."

hints: The answer for a node is a new node, so decide what the answer for each child is before combining them.
Compare the two pictures level by level. Which nodes moved, and which nodes had their own children reordered?
Build a new node with the same label whose children are the mirrored children, taken from last to first.

exercises.title: Search: the first path to a label
exercises.prompt_md:
Implement `find_path(t, target)`. Search left to right and depth first, and return the list of labels from the root down to the **first** node whose label equals `target`. If the root itself matches, the answer is a one-element list. If no node matches, return `None`.

The starter already calls `show_try(whole, path, target)` when a call begins, so each frame shows one node being examined. Keep that call first, and pass `path + (i,)` and `whole` when you descend. Stop as soon as a match is found: a correct search for 9 in the demo examines four nodes and never looks at the second 9 or at -3. Predict the returned list before you press Run.

checklist.step: Return the first matching path, or None
Examine nodes in order and stop at the match

tests.name: first_match_paths
tests.code:
show_try = lambda *args: None
assert find_path(tree(6), 6) == [6], "When the root matches, the path is the one-element list holding the root's label."
assert find_path(tree(6), 7) is None, "Return None when no node carries the target."
assert find_path(tree(1, [tree(0, [tree(0)])]), 0) == [1, 0], "A label of 0 is a real match; stop at the first one."
got = find_path(tree(1, [tree(2, [tree(5)]), tree(5)]), 5)
assert got == [1, 2, 5], f"Depth first, left to right: the 5 under child 0 comes before the root's own second child. Got {got}."
assert find_path(tree(1, [tree(2), tree(3, [tree(4)])]), 4) == [1, 3, 4], "After a child's subtree fails, continue with the next child."

import random
rng = random.Random(645)
def make(depth):
    return tree(rng.randrange(-4, 5), [make(depth - 1) for _ in range(rng.randrange(4))] if depth else [])

def oracle(t, target):
    if t["value"] == target: return [t["value"]]
    for c in t["children"]:
        found = oracle(c, target)
        if found is not None: return [t["value"]] + found
    return None
for _ in range(60):
    t = make(4); target = rng.randrange(-5, 6)
    got = find_path(t, target)
    assert got == oracle(t, target), f"On a random hierarchy with repeated labels, looking for {target}: expected {oracle(t, target)}, got {got}."

tests.name: visited_order
tests.code:
from scimigo import _frame_count, _frame
def visited(target):
    before = _frame_count()
    result = find_path(sample, target)
    names = []
    for f in range(before, _frame_count()):
        figures = [o for o in _frame(f) if o['kind'] == 'figure']
        assert figures, "Every frame of the search should draw the hierarchy (call show_try)."
        names.extend(figures[0]['params']['highlights'])
    return result, names
result, names = visited(9)
assert result == [4, 0, 9], f"The first 9 lies under child 1: expected [4, 0, 9], got {result}."
assert names == ['root:4', '0:7', '1:0', '1.0:9'], f"A search for 9 examines root, 0, 1 and 1.0, then stops. Yours examined {names}."
result, names = visited(-8)
assert result is None, "No node is labelled -8, so the result is None."
assert names == ['root:4', '0:7', '1:0', '1.0:9', '1.1:9', '2:-3'], f"A failed search examines every node once, parents before children. Yours examined {names}."
result, names = visited(4)
assert result == [4] and names == ['root:4'], f"A match at the root examines one node and returns [4]. Got {result} after {names}."

hints: A search call answers one question about its own subtree: the path to the first match here, or None.
Check the current node before its children. Then look at what a child's call returns and decide whether to go on to the next child.
If a child reports a path, put the current label in front of it and return at once. Return None only after every child has reported None.

exercises.title: Measure: reads per node
exercises.prompt_md:
Implement `profile(t)`: visit the whole hierarchy, read every node's label exactly once with `label(node)`, and return the number of label reads your traversal actually made. Use `branches` to descend. Count the reads as they happen; the checks replace `label` with a counting version and compare its count with yours on sizes and shapes the demo does not use.

The demo measures three sizes and draws your numbers as bars. Drawing happens after the measurement, so it is not part of the count. Before running, predict the ratio of reads to nodes.

questions.prompt: If each node supplies one label read, what is reads divided by n?

choices.why: Depth bounds a path, not all visited nodes.
Internal nodes also supply label reads.
n reads divided by n nodes equals 1.

checklist.step: Count the label reads that actually happen
Measure three sizes and draw the counts

tests.name: fresh_measurements
tests.code:
show_measure=lambda *args: None
original_label=label
observed=[0]
def counted(node):
    observed[0]+=1
    return original_label(node)
label=counted
for n in [7,19,53,211]:
    observed[0]=0
    value=profile(make_star(n))
    assert value==observed[0], f"profile reported {value} reads but made {observed[0]}: report the reads that happened, not a stored number."
    assert value==n, f"A hierarchy of {n} nodes needs {n} label reads, one per node; yours made {value}."
t={'value':4,'children':[make_star(9),make_star(12),{'value':1,'children':[{'value':2,'children':[make_star(5)]}]}]}
observed[0]=0
value=profile(t)
assert value==observed[0]==29, f"On a deeper 29-node hierarchy profile reported {value} and made {observed[0]} reads: descend below the first level."

tests.name: measured_bars
tests.code:
from scimigo import _frame_count, _frame
before=_frame_count()
rows=[(n,profile(make_star(n))) for n in (9,27,81)]
assert rows==[(9,9),(27,27),(81,81)], f"Measured (n, reads) rows should be [(9, 9), (27, 27), (81, 81)]; yours are {rows}."
show_measure(rows)
assert _frame_count()-before==1, "show_measure should record exactly one frame."
objects=_frame(before)
bars=[o for o in objects if o['kind']=='rectangle']
assert len(bars)==3, "Draw a bar for each measured row."
for bar,(n,c) in zip(bars,rows):
    assert abs(bar['width']-430*c/81)<1e-6, f"The bar for n={n} should be proportional to its {c} reads."
    assert any(o['kind']=='text' and o['value']=='n='+str(n) for o in objects), f"Label the bar for n={n}."
    assert any(o['kind']=='text' and o['value'].startswith('reads='+str(c)+',') for o in objects), f"Show the measured count {c} beside its bar."

hints: A measurement counts events while the traversal runs; it is not computed from the input size.
Find the one place where your traversal reads a label, and make sure every node passes through it once.
Keep a counter outside the recursive helper, add one beside each label read, visit each child, and return the counter.

exercises.title: Mastery challenge: charges for nested shipments
exercises.prompt_md:
A shipping manifest contains packages inside packages. A terminal record stores its charge in its numeric label (negative values represent credits); a containing record has a label but no additional charge. Produce a dictionary from each child-index position to the total terminal charge enclosed there. The outer position is `()`; its second child is `(1,)`. Include every record, even when labels repeat or charges are zero. The supplied version is correct but repeatedly inspects the same records. For manifests with 127 records in a long nesting chain, use no more than six child-list inspections per record. The demo draws the outer charge. Explain your reasoning after your first attempt.

The inspection budget measures traversal work only. Constructing and storing child-index paths also costs space and time proportional to the total length of the reported paths.

questions.prompt: What must an efficient report preserve?

choices.why: Positions distinguish records with equal labels.
Only terminal labels are charges.
Discarding completed amounts forces repeated work.

questions.prompt: What does a completed amount represent?

choices.why: A child may itself contain packages.
It includes each terminal record in that region once.
Containing records have no additional charge.

questions.prompt: What growth should record inspections have?

choices.why: Reusing completed information avoids depth-dependent repeated scans.
This matches repeated scans of a long chain.
Every terminal charge may affect the result.

questions.prompt: What happens when each enclosing package scans everything it contains?

choices.why: The same inner records remain enclosed by many packages.
The charges stay the same; the repeated work changes.
With 5 nested records, full scans inspect 5+4+3+2+1=15 records instead of 5.

checklist.step: Produce the charge for every record position
Avoid repeated inspection of completed records

tests.name: all_positions
tests.code:
show=lambda *args: None
import random
rng=random.Random(760)
def make(depth):
    return tree(rng.randrange(-3,15),[make(depth-1) for _ in range(rng.randrange(4))] if depth else [])
def expected(t,path=(),out=None):
    out={} if out is None else out
    children=t['children']
    value=t['value'] if not children else sum(expected(c,path+(i,),out)[path+(i,)] for i,c in enumerate(children))
    out[path]=value
    return out
for _ in range(35):
    t=make(4)
    assert charges(t)==expected(t), "Include every position, charge only terminal records, and preserve equal-labelled positions."
assert charges(tree(90,[tree(2),tree(3)]))[()]==5, "Container labels are not additional charges."
assert charges(tree(-6))=={(): -6}, "A manifest with one terminal record reports that record's own charge at ()."
